run.question: My AWS Lambda function 'payment-processor' in us-east-1 has high latency issues. Investigate why.

report.summary: The subject asked about an AWS Lambda function 'payment-processor' in us-east-1. No AWS/CloudWatch source is configured for this Run (available sources are jaeger, knowledge, kubernetes, prometheus; not_integrated lists change_history only), so no Lambda Duration, InitDuration, ConcurrentExecutions, memory or CloudWatch Logs data could be read, and the target cluster is an OpenTelemetry-demo Kubernetes cluster, not Lambda. I fetched runbook skill_id lambda-performance-troubleshooting and tried each of its steps: Step 1 (CloudWatch Duration metrics) not carried out — no CloudWatch/AWS tool exists in this Run; Step 2 (CloudWatch Logs error/timeout filter) not carried out — no CloudWatch Logs tool; I instead read the analogous Kubernetes pod logs of the closest-named workload; Step 3 (InitDuration cold starts) not carried out — no CloudWatch; Step 4 (ConcurrentExecutions) not carried out — no CloudWatch; Step 5 (memory utilisation / CloudWatch Logs Insights REPORT fields) not carried out — no CloudWatch Logs Insights; the analogous Kubernetes check (memory limit and restarts) found a 120Mi memory limit and zero restarts. No object named 'payment-processor' exists in the cluster: the cluster-wide deployment list (24 objects) and pod list (32 objects) contain no such name; the similarly named entity is Deployment/Service 'payment' in namespace otel-demo (image ghcr.io/open-telemetry/demo:2.0.2-payment), which is a different entity and is not evidence about the Lambda function. That payment workload looks healthy on the signals I could read: single pod Running and ready with 0 restarts, and its charge handling completes in about 1 ms per request pair in its own logs at level info. All Prometheus and Jaeger calls in this Run returned SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE, so no latency series or trace could be obtained for any service — the reported high latency is therefore neither confirmed nor refuted, and no root cause can be named.

claims.text: The cluster-wide deployment list returned 24 deployments and the cluster-wide pod list returned 32 pods; neither contains an object named 'payment-processor'. The only similarly named workloads are Deployment 'payment' and Service 'payment' in namespace otel-demo (image ghcr.io/open-telemetry/demo:2.0.2-payment, ClusterIP port 8080), which are different entities from the named AWS Lambda function.

Pod payment-6f7bc865d6-wwqnm in namespace otel-demo is Running, its single container 'payment' is ready with restartCount 0 and running since 2026-11-23T14:36:52Z, and it is owned by ReplicaSet payment-6f7bc865d6.

In the 100 newest of 192 log lines read from the payment container (timestamps 2026-11-23T15:53:45Z to 2026-11-23T16:24:26Z), every line is level 'info' and each 'Charge request received.' line is followed by a 'Transaction complete.' line for the same trace_id within roughly 1 ms (for example trace 8e57c8196b10c9fe802705a49054cab4 at 15:53:45.752Z and 15:53:45.753Z).

The payment Deployment's container runs with only a memory limit of 120Mi and carries feature-flag env vars FLAGD_HOST=flagd and FLAGD_PORT=8013 alongside OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://$(OTEL_COLLECTOR_NAME):4317.

ConfigMap flagd-config in namespace otel-demo declares fault-injection flags 'paymentFailure' ("Fail payment service charge requests n%") and 'paymentUnreachable' ("Payment service is unavailable"), both with state ENABLED and defaultVariant "off"; every other flag in the same ConfigMap (productCatalogFailure, recommendationCacheFailure, adManualGc, adHighCpu, adFailure, kafkaQueueProblems, cartFailure, loadGeneratorFloodHomepage, imageSlowLoad) also has defaultVariant "off".

For the Kubernetes payment workload (a different entity from the named Lambda), the pod state and logs I could read show no failure signal: 0 restarts, container ready, and only info-level charge/transaction pairs; this does not address latency, which could not be measured because Prometheus and Jaeger were unreachable in this Run.

Rejected as a supported explanation: that the feature-flag fault settings in ConfigMap flagd-config were actively injecting payment failures or delays. Both payment-related flags declare defaultVariant "off" and no other flag declares an active variant, and no event or object was seen applying a change to the payment workload. The flags' runtime-evaluated values are not observable from here, so this cannot be fully excluded.

The reported high latency most likely belongs to an AWS-hosted Lambda function whose telemetry lives in CloudWatch; no CloudWatch/AWS source is configured in this Run, so the latency cannot be measured, baselined or attributed from the available data and no cause can be named here.

Provide the CloudWatch (metrics and logs) integration for the AWS account/region us-east-1, then re-run the fetched runbook lambda-performance-troubleshooting steps against function 'payment-processor': p95/p99 Duration against a comparable earlier baseline, InitDuration/cold-start counts, ConcurrentExecutions/throttles, and @maxMemoryUsed versus configured memory.

Restore or re-register the Prometheus and Jaeger sources for target m0-otel-20260909 so latency series (e.g. traces_span_metrics_calls_total, rpc_client_duration_milliseconds, http_server_request_duration_seconds) and traces for service 'payment' can be queried; without them any latency statement about the Kubernetes services would be unverified.

gaps: No AWS/CloudWatch data source is available in this Run (only jaeger, kubernetes, prometheus and knowledge are listed as available; not_integrated lists change_history), so nothing about the Lambda function 'payment-processor' in us-east-1 — its Duration, InitDuration, ConcurrentExecutions, memory usage or CloudWatch logs — could be read.

Every Prometheus call in this Run (get_metric_names, get_all_labels, get_prometheus_target, execute_prometheus_instant_query, metrics_range_query) returned status error SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE, and every Jaeger call (traces_list_services, traces_search) returned SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE; therefore no error-rate, latency or trace evidence exists for any service in this assessment, and the absence of such signal is not evidence of health.

The cluster-wide events query (kubernetes_jq_query kind=events, grouped by involvedObject.kind/namespace/reason over the authorized window 2026-10-24T16:24:51Z to 2026-11-23T16:24:51Z, no type filter) returned zero items, so no event-based evidence of restarts, evictions, OOMKills or probe failures was obtained; that query matched nothing, it does not prove nothing happened.

The payment container's 'previous' log stream was unavailable (HTTP 400, no previous terminated container), so only the current container's logs from 2026-11-23T15:53:45Z to 16:24:26Z were read, and 92 older lines of 192 were cut by the limit.
Whether the flagd flags paymentFailure/paymentUnreachable were overridden at runtime by flagd is unknown; only the ConfigMap defaults ("off") were readable.

Secrets are unreadable, and no application-level latency measurement (server-side or client-observed) exists for the payment service in the evidence gathered, so its true request latency is unknown rather than zero.
next_steps: Add a read-only CloudWatch integration (us-east-1) for the AWS Lambda namespace and the 'payment-processor' log group so Duration, InitDuration, ConcurrentExecutions, Throttles and memory-utilisation data become queryable.

Once CloudWatch is available, compare the function's Duration p95/p99 and InitDuration during the incident window with an equivalent earlier baseline period, and check for a cold-start or concurrency-throttle signature.
Verify the function's dependencies (downstream HTTP/gRPC calls, VPC/ENI configuration, layer size and configured memory) for added init or per-invocation time.
Restore the Prometheus read-only endpoint and Jaeger query service so Kubernetes-service latency and traces can corroborate or exclude an application-side cause.

content.name: lambda-performance-troubleshooting
content.content:
# AWS Lambda High Latency Troubleshooting

## Overview
This runbook helps diagnose and resolve AWS Lambda function performance issues including high latency, timeouts, and cold starts.

## Steps

### Step 1: Query Performance Metrics
Use CloudWatch to check Lambda function latency over time:
```
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace <lambda-namespace> \
  --metric-name Duration --dimensions Name=FunctionName,Value=<function-name> \
  --statistics Average,Maximum --start-time <start-time> \
  --end-time <end-time> --period 300
```

### Step 2: Check Function Logs
Look for errors or slow operations in CloudWatch Logs:
```bash
aws logs filter-log-events --log-group-name <lambda-log-group>/<function-name> \
  --filter-pattern "[ERROR] OR [WARN] OR timeout" --limit 100
```

### Step 3: Analyze Cold Start Patterns
Query CloudWatch for cold start frequency:
```
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace <lambda-namespace> \
  --metric-name InitDuration --dimensions Name=FunctionName,Value=<function-name> \
  --statistics Average,Count --start-time <start-time> \
  --end-time <end-time> --period 300
```

### Step 4: Check Concurrent Executions
Verify Lambda isn't hitting concurrency limits:
```
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace <lambda-namespace> \
  --metric-name ConcurrentExecutions --dimensions Name=FunctionName,Value=<function-name> \
  --statistics Maximum --start-time <start-time> \
  --end-time <end-time> --period 60
```

### Step 5: Review Memory Utilization
Check if function needs more memory allocation:
```bash
aws logs insights start-query --log-group-name <lambda-log-group>/<function-name> \
  --start-time <epoch-start> --end-time <epoch-end> \
  --query-string "fields @timestamp, @message | filter @type = 'REPORT' | stats max(@maxMemoryUsed), avg(@memorySize)"
```
